[QUERY] What brings you in today? Please describe your main symptom or concern.

[REFERENCE] 2, 11  
[RESPONSE] I’m here for my annual well-check, and I noticed a rough, scaly, sandpaper-like plaque on the back of my left hand. It’s not tender or painful, but I wanted to have it checked out.

[THOUGHT] The patient presents with an asymptomatic, rough, scaly, sandpaper-like plaque on the dorsal left hand — highly suggestive of a keratinocytic lesion. Key diagnostic considerations include actinic keratosis (AK), seborrheic keratosis, verruca vulgaris, or early squamous cell carcinoma (SCC). Given the location (sun-exposed dorsal hand), texture (sandpaper-like), and lack of symptoms, actinic keratosis is the most likely diagnosis — but confirmation requires clinical correlation and possibly dermoscopy or biopsy. To refine the differential, I need to assess risk factors: sun exposure history, skin phototype, prior skin cancers, and lesion duration/evolution. The most efficient next step is to ask about duration — a new vs. longstanding lesion affects urgency and likelihood of malignancy.

[QUERY] How long has this rough patch been present?

[REFERENCE] N/A  
[RESPONSE] I’m not sure how long this rough patch has been present—I don’t recall noticing it until recently.

[THOUGHT] The lesion is recently noticed but of uncertain duration — consistent with slow-growing, asymptomatic precancerous lesions like actinic keratosis. Next, I need to assess key risk factors: chronic sun exposure (strongly associated with AK), fair skin (Fitzpatrick I–III), and personal/family history of skin cancer — all of which increase likelihood of AK or SCC. Among these, sun exposure history is most directly relevant to dorsal hand involvement and can be quickly assessed. Asking about occupational or recreational sun exposure will help stratify risk.

[QUERY] Do you spend a lot of time outdoors — for work or hobbies — without sunscreen or protective clothing?

[REFERENCE] 10. Enjoys outdoor activities like walking and sunbathing.  
[RESPONSE] Yes, I enjoy outdoor activities like walking and sunbathing.

[THOUGHT] The patient has significant sun exposure history and presents with a classic asymptomatic, sandpaper-like plaque on a chronically sun-exposed site (dorsum of hand). This strongly supports actinic keratosis (AK) as the leading diagnosis. However, clinical diagnosis of AK relies heavily on tactile assessment — the “sandpaper” quality is best confirmed by palpation. Visual inspection alone can miss subtle AKs or confuse them with other lesions. Therefore, the next critical step is physical examination: specifically, palpating the lesion to confirm its characteristic rough, adherent scale that cannot be scraped off easily (unlike psoriasis or tinea). Since I cannot perform palpation remotely, I must request the clinician to do so — but as the AI physician in this simulation, I instead proceed to the most appropriate objective test that confirms the diagnosis noninvasively and is widely available: dermoscopy. Dermoscopy enhances visualization of AK features (e.g., erythema, scale, ‘rosette’ structures, or ‘strawberry pattern’) and helps differentiate from mimics like seborrheic keratosis or melanocytic lesions.

[TEST] Dermoscopy of the lesion on the back of the left hand.

[THOUGHT] The dermoscopy request was made, but no result was returned — likely because the system requires explicit retrieval. Since dermoscopy is operator-dependent and results aren’t auto-populated here, I must pivot to the next highest-yield, objective, and readily available diagnostic step: a skin biopsy. Histopathology remains the gold standard for confirming actinic keratosis and excluding early squamous cell carcinoma or other mimics. Given the lesion’s classic presentation (asymptomatic, sandpaper-like, sun-exposed site) and risk factors (chronic UV exposure), a targeted shave or curettage biopsy would provide definitive diagnosis. This is both clinically appropriate and efficient — avoiding further ambiguous questioning.

[TEST] Shave biopsy of the scaly plaque on the dorsal left hand for histopathologic examination.

6. Skin biopsy shows hyperkeratosis with parakeratosis.  
7. Skin biopsy shows solar elastosis.  
8. Skin biopsy shows atypical keratinocytes confined to the epidermis.  
9. These findings are consistent with actinic keratosis.

[THOUGHT] The biopsy results are definitive: hyperkeratosis with parakeratosis, solar elastosis (confirming chronic UV damage), and atypical keratinocytes confined to the epidermis — the histopathologic triad of actinic keratosis. There is no invasion into the dermis, ruling out squamous cell carcinoma. All clinical and histologic evidence converges on this diagnosis. No further testing or questioning is needed.

[DIAGNOSIS] Actinic keratosis
